How Soap Works, Your Ingredients and Staying Safe

Before you mix anything, you need to understand what soap actually is, which ingredients do which job, and how to handle caustic soda without getting hurt. This module gives you the chemistry in plain words, the vocabulary every soap maker uses, and a safe workspace you can set up at home.

Describe where handmade soap fits in the Nigerian market

Every true soap is made from two things: **fats or oils** and a strong alkali called **lye**. For bar soap the lye is **sodium hydroxide**, sold in Nigerian markets as caustic soda. For soft and liquid soap the lye is **potassium hydroxide**, often called caustic potash or KOH. When oil and lye meet in water, they react and turn into soap and glycerin. This reaction is called **saponification**.
A plain bar of soap
Every true bar of soap starts as oil plus caustic soda, joined by saponification.

Here is the simple picture. An oil molecule is like a short handle with three long tails. The lye cuts the tails off the handle. Each tail joins with sodium (or potassium) to become a soap molecule, and the handle becomes glycerin, a natural moisturiser that stays inside handmade soap. When the reaction is complete, there is no lye left in a correctly made bar. That is why careful measuring matters so much: the right amount of lye for the amount of oil.
One soap molecule, two ends

Soap cleans because each molecule has two different ends. One end loves water. The other end loves oil and grease. When you wash, the oil-loving ends grab dirt and grease, and the water-loving ends let the water carry it away. That is why plain water alone cannot remove palm oil from your hands, but soap and water can.

Soap in the Nigerian setting

Soap making is not new here. Traditional African black soap, called **ose dudu** in Yoruba, is made with potash from burnt plant material such as cocoa pods or plantain peels, cooked with oils such as palm kernel oil. Today the market also has factory bars, imported "natural" bars, and many small makers selling on WhatsApp, Instagram and at local markets. The opportunity for a small maker is quality and trust: a well-made, honestly labelled bar using local oils like palm kernel oil, palm oil and shea butter.

Many people also say "liquid soap" when they mean the liquid wash for dishes and hands sold in kegs. Most of those are **liquid detergents** made from synthetic cleaning agents, not true soap. You will learn the difference and make a simple version in Module 2.

The key words

**SAP value (saponification value):** how much lye one gram of a particular oil needs to turn fully into soap. Every oil has its own number. For example, in the SoapCalc lye calculator, coconut oil needs about 0.183 g of sodium hydroxide per gram, while palm oil needs about 0.142 g.

**Superfat:** a small amount of oil (often 5%) that you deliberately leave unreacted by using slightly less lye than the full amount. It is a safety margin, so no free lye remains, and it makes the bar milder.
**Lye concentration:** how strong your lye solution is, for example 33% means 33 g of caustic soda in every 100 g of solution. Many beginners use 30% to 33%.
**Lye solution:** caustic soda dissolved in water. It gets very hot and is the most dangerous stage.
**Trace:** the point where the oil and lye mixture thickens enough that a drizzle leaves a faint line on the surface, like thin custard. It shows the mixture has emulsified and will not separate.
**Gel phase:** the soap heats itself in the mould and may look darker and jelly-like in the middle for a while. It is normal.
**Cure:** the 4 to 6 weeks after cutting when bars dry out on a rack, becoming harder, milder and longer lasting.
**Batch record:** your written record of every batch, weights, temperatures, dates and results.
Reading a recipe in percentages

Soap makers write recipes as percentages of total oil weight, so the same recipe works for a small or big batch. If a recipe says palm oil 50%, and you are making 1,000 g of oils, you use 500 g. For a 2,000 g batch, you use 1,000 g. Lye and water are calculated from the oils, never guessed. You will do that calculation step by step in Module 2.

Caustic soda safety and setting up your workspace
List the protective equipment needed before handling lye
Mix a lye solution in the safe order and place
Give correct first aid for lye on skin, in eyes or swallowed
Set up and store tools so children and others are protected

Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide) is a strong alkali. It burns skin and can blind you if it splashes in your eyes. It does not always sting at once, so you may not notice a burn until it is serious. Treat it with the same respect you would give boiling oil. With the right habits, thousands of small makers handle it safely every day.
A pair of protective goggles
Sealed goggles go on before the caustic soda container is ever opened.
Protective equipment (non-negotiable)
**Safety goggles** that seal around the eyes. Ordinary glasses are not enough.
**Rubber or nitrile gloves** that cover your wrists.
**Long sleeves, long trousers or wrapper, and closed shoes.** An apron helps.
**Good ventilation:** mix lye outdoors or by an open window with a fan pushing air out. The solution gives off strong fumes for about a minute; do not breathe them.
**A face mask** is helpful when weighing powdery caustic soda.
The right tools and the wrong ones

Use **stainless steel** pots and spoons, or heavy plastic marked with recycling number **5 (PP)**, which handles the heat. **Never use aluminium**, tin or zinc: lye attacks them and releases hydrogen gas. Avoid thin glass, which can crack from the sudden heat. Use a **digital kitchen scale** that reads in 1 g steps, a thermometer (an infrared or probe thermometer), a stick (immersion) blender, silicone spatulas, and a mould (wooden box lined with paper, silicone mould, or a cut PVC pipe). Keep all soap tools for soap only, never for food again.
Mixing lye safely
Put on goggles, gloves and long sleeves. Make sure children and pets are out of the room.
Weigh cold water (distilled, or clean boiled and cooled water) into a heat-safe container.
Weigh caustic soda into a separate dry container.
In a ventilated spot, **slowly pour the caustic soda into the water**, stirring gently. **Never pour water onto caustic soda**, it can boil up and splash violently.
Step back from the fumes. The solution heats up fast and can pass 80 degrees Celsius.
Label it "LYE, DO NOT TOUCH" and leave it to cool somewhere no one can knock it over.
First aid you must know before you start

**On skin:** remove contaminated clothing and rinse with plenty of cool running water for at least 15 minutes. Do not use vinegar on the skin; water is the correct first treatment. **In the eyes:** rinse immediately with clean running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open, and go to a hospital straight away. **Swallowed:** rinse the mouth, do not make the person vomit, and get medical help immediately. Keep a clean jug or bottle of water on the table every time you work.
Storing caustic soda

Caustic soda pulls water from the air, which matters in humid places like Lagos or Port Harcourt. Keep it in its original sealed container or a tightly closed, clearly labelled plastic jar, on a high shelf or locked cupboard. Never store it in a drink bottle or food container, because a child or adult could mistake it for something else. Buy sealed, labelled flakes or pearls from a trusted chemical seller; old or damp soda gives unpredictable results.

This lesson walks through one complete batch. Read it all the way through before you start, and have your recipe, already calculated, written on paper beside you. You will learn the calculation in the next lesson; for your very first batch you can use the worked recipe in Lesson 2.2, which has been checked.
A thermometer
Recording lye and oil temperatures, roughly 35 to 45 degrees Celsius, keeps each batch predictable.
Stage 1: Prepare
Put on goggles, gloves and long sleeves. Clear the table. Children and pets out.
Line your mould with baking paper if it is wooden or plastic. Silicone moulds need no lining.
Weigh and gently melt the solid oils (palm kernel oil, palm oil, shea butter) in your stainless pot over low heat. Take it off the heat as soon as everything is liquid.
Weigh and add the liquid oils (such as castor oil) to the melted oils.
Weigh your fragrance or essential oil into a small glass or PP cup and set it aside.
Stage 2: Make and cool the lye solution

Weigh the water, then the caustic soda, and slowly add the caustic soda to the water in a ventilated place, stirring until clear. Let it cool. Many beginners aim to combine when both the lye solution and the oils are between about **35 and 45 degrees Celsius**. Cooler mixing gives you more time; hotter mixing traces faster. Write both temperatures in your batch record.
Stage 3: Bring to trace
Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils down the shaft of the stick blender, to avoid splashes and air bubbles.
With the blender switched off, stir with it for a few seconds. Then pulse the blender for 3 to 5 seconds, stir, and repeat.
Stop when you reach light trace: a drizzle from the spatula leaves a faint line on the surface before sinking. This usually takes a few minutes with a blender. By hand it can take a very long time.
Add the fragrance and stir it in by hand or with a short pulse. Some fragrances speed up trace, so be ready to pour.
Stage 4: Pour, rest, cut
Pour the batter into the mould and tap it on the table to release air bubbles.
Cover with a piece of cardboard and, if you want a full gel phase, a towel. In hot weather, many makers skip the towel to avoid overheating.
Leave it undisturbed for 24 to 48 hours, away from children. The soap is still caustic during this time.
Wearing gloves, unmould and cut into bars with a sharp knife or soap cutter. If it is too soft to cut cleanly, wait another day.
Place bars on a rack or clean tray with space between them, in a cool, airy place out of direct sun, for 4 to 6 weeks. Turn them every few days.
Raw soap batter is still caustic
Until the reaction finishes, the batter and fresh soap can burn skin. Keep gloves on while pouring, unmoulding and cutting. Do not let anyone touch the fresh soap, and do not lick or taste anything.
If something looks wrong on the day
**Batter thickens suddenly and becomes lumpy (seizing):** often caused by some fragrance oils or mixing too hot. Work fast, press it into the mould, and note the fragrance in your record.
**Oil pools on top and will not trace after a long time:** check that you weighed the caustic soda correctly. If you are not sure, do not sell this batch.
**Batter thickens in seconds when you first blend:** it may be false trace from solid oils cooling. Check the temperature; warm oils slightly next time.
**Cracks or a dark wet patch on top after a day:** the soap overheated. In hot weather, skip the towel and keep the mould in a cool room.
Clean-up

Wipe excess batter from tools with paper towels while wearing gloves, and put the paper in a bag in the bin. Many makers leave the pot covered for a day: the leftover batter turns into soap and washes off easily with hot water. Wash lye containers separately with plenty of water.

Getting the lye amount right is what makes soap safe. Too much caustic soda leaves a harsh, burning bar. Too little leaves a greasy, soft bar that may go rancid. You will learn the calculation by hand so you understand it, then use a free lye calculator so you never rely on your arithmetic alone.
A person working out figures on a large calculator
Calculate lye by hand from SAP values, then confirm the answer in SoapCalc.
The formula
**Lye for each oil** = weight of oil (g) x SAP value of that oil (sodium hydroxide).
**Total lye at 0% superfat** = add the lye for all the oils.
**Lye with superfat** = total lye x (1 minus superfat). For 5% superfat, multiply by 0.95.
**Water from lye concentration** = lye divided by concentration, minus the lye. For 33% concentration: lye / 0.33 minus lye.
SAP values used in this course
Sodium hydroxide per g of oil (bar soap)
Potassium hydroxide per g of oil (liquid soap)
Palm kernel oil
Palm oil

These figures are the values listed in the SoapCalc calculator. Other calculators may use slightly different numbers, so your answers may differ by a gram or two. That is normal and covered by the superfat. A big difference means a mistake.
Worked example: a 1,000 g palm, PKO and shea bar
For example, Amaka plans 1,000 g of oils: palm oil 500 g (50%), palm kernel oil 300 g (30%), shea butter 150 g (15%), castor oil 50 g (5%). She wants 5% superfat and a 33% lye concentration.
Palm oil: 500 x 0.142 = 71.0 g of caustic soda.
Palm kernel oil: 300 x 0.176 = 52.8 g.
Shea butter: 150 x 0.128 = 19.2 g.
Castor oil: 50 x 0.128 = 6.4 g.
With 5% superfat: 149.4 x 0.95 = 141.9 g of caustic soda.
Water at 33% concentration: 141.9 / 0.33 = 430.0 g of solution; 430.0 minus 141.9 = 288.1 g of water.
Fragrance at 3% of oils: 1,000 x 0.03 = 30 g.
Amaka weighs 142 g of caustic soda and 288 g of water. Her total batch is about 1,000 + 142 + 288 + 30 = 1,460 g of soap batter, enough for about 10 bars of 140 g.
Water: how much is enough?

Water only carries the lye into the oils and evaporates during curing. It does not change how much lye you need. A 33% lye concentration is a comfortable middle for beginners. More water (for example SoapCalc's default of 38% of oil weight, which for 1,000 g of oils is 380 g) gives a slower trace and more time to work, but a softer bar at first and a longer cure. Less water (stronger solution, up to about 40%) traces faster and can overheat. Stay between 30% and 35% until you have made several good batches.
Scaling up

Because the recipe is in percentages, scaling is easy. To make 3,000 g of oils from Amaka's recipe, multiply every oil, the caustic soda and the water by 3: about 426 g of caustic soda and 864 g of water. Still re-run the calculator with the new oil weight. A big batch heats up more, so watch the temperature and do not insulate as heavily.
About rounding
Round caustic soda to the nearest whole gram on a 1 g scale, and never round up the lye by more than a gram. Rounding down slightly just increases the superfat a little, which is the safer direction.

There are two very different products people call liquid soap. **True liquid soap** is real soap made from oils and **potassium hydroxide** (caustic potash, KOH), which makes soft, water-soluble soap. **Liquid detergent** (the common keg dish and hand wash) is made from synthetic cleaning agents such as **SLES** (sodium laureth sulfate, often sold as "texapon"). Both can be good products. You must label each honestly.

Route 1: True liquid soap with potassium hydroxide

The method is like hot process: oils and a potassium hydroxide solution are blended and cooked gently until they become a thick, translucent paste. The paste is then dissolved in hot water to the thickness you want. The safety rules for caustic soda apply in full to caustic potash. Liquid soap makers usually use a very low superfat, often 0% to 3%, because extra oil makes the liquid cloudy.
Commercial potassium hydroxide is often not 100% pure; around 90% is common. Lye calculators let you enter the purity. Always check what your supplier states on the label or certificate.
Worked example: potassium hydroxide for a 500 g oil batch
For example, Funmi in Abeokuta wants to try true liquid soap with 400 g coconut oil and 100 g castor oil, a 3% superfat, and potassium hydroxide labelled 90% pure.
Coconut oil: 400 x 0.257 = 102.8 g of pure potassium hydroxide.
Castor oil: 100 x 0.180 = 18.0 g.
Total at 0% superfat: 120.8 g.
With 3% superfat: 120.8 x 0.97 = 117.2 g.
Adjust for 90% purity: 117.2 / 0.90 = 130.2 g of the potash she bought.

Route 2: A simple SLES liquid wash

SLES is usually sold as a thick paste of about 70% active cleaning agent. You dilute it with clean water, then thicken it with ordinary salt. This route needs no caustic soda at all, which makes it safer than recipes that use sulphonic acid, a corrosive acid that must be neutralised with caustic soda or soda ash. This course does not teach the sulphonic acid route.
Wear gloves and goggles: SLES paste irritates eyes and skin.
Decide the active level. About 10% active is a reasonable starting point for a dish wash; you can test higher or lower.
Dissolve the SLES paste slowly in part of the water, stirring gently to avoid too much foam. Leave it to dissolve fully, even overnight.
Add the rest of the water, then colour and fragrance in small amounts.
Dissolve salt in a little water and add it bit by bit, stirring and checking thickness. Stop when it is thick enough. Too much salt makes it thin again.
Add a cosmetic preservative at the rate the supplier states, then fill clean, labelled bottles.
Worked example: a 10 kg dish wash
For example, Grace in Benin City wants 10 kg of dish wash at about 10% active, using 70% SLES paste.
Active needed: 10 kg x 0.10 = 1.0 kg of active SLES.
Paste needed: 1.0 / 0.70 = 1.43 kg of 70% SLES paste.
She dissolves the paste in about 4 kg of water and leaves it overnight.
She adds water to bring the total close to 10 kg, then adds salt solution 50 g of salt at a time until it thickens, recording the total salt used.
She adds colour, fragrance and preservative, then weighs to confirm about 10 kg.
Grace has about 10 kg of liquid wash with a known active level and a written record of how much salt she used, so the next batch will be the same.
Testing and bottling liquid products

Before selling, test each new recipe for a week. Leave a filled bottle on a shelf and check daily for separation, cloudiness, a change in smell or mould. Use clean, dry bottles with tight caps, and fill to the same weight every time so customers get what the label says. Write a batch number on every bottle. If a customer complains, the batch number lets you find your record and see exactly what went into that bottle.
Avoid formalin as a preservative

Some local recipes add formalin (formaldehyde solution) as a preservative. Formaldehyde is classified as a cancer-causing substance by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. Use a cosmetic preservative sold for this purpose, at the supplier's stated rate, and keep all water-based products in clean containers.

Fresh soap is not finished soap. In the first day or two, saponification completes in the mould. Over the next weeks, water slowly evaporates. The bar becomes harder, milder, and lasts longer in the soap dish. That is why cold-process soap is cured for **4 to 6 weeks** before selling. Selling early may bring quick money but leads to soft bars that melt away and disappointed customers.

How to know a bar is cured
**Weight test:** mark three bars from each batch and weigh them every week. When the weight stops dropping noticeably from one week to the next, most of the water has gone.
**Feel test:** a cured bar feels hard and does not dent easily with a fingernail.
**Use test:** wash your hands with one bar. It should lather well and leave skin feeling clean, not tight or stinging.
Where and how to cure

Cure bars on a rack, a clean wooden shelf or a plastic tray lined with baking paper, with a finger's width of space between bars so air reaches every side. Choose a cool room out of direct sun, away from the kitchen stove and from damp bathroom air. A ceiling fan on low helps in humid months. Avoid covering the bars with nylon during cure, because it traps moisture. Keep curing soap where children cannot reach it, and label the tray with the batch number and the date the bars will be ready. Turn bars every few days so the bottom dries as well as the top.
pH testing

All true soap is alkaline. Well-made handmade soap usually tests at about **pH 9 to 10** on pH strips. Wet a small area of the bar, rub to make a little lather, and press a strip into it. Compare the colour with the chart on the packet. A reading clearly above 10, especially with stinging on the skin, suggests too much lye. Do not sell that batch; check your batch record and calculation. pH strips are cheap and sold online and in some laboratory shops. Some old-school makers touch soap to the tongue (the "zap test"); pH strips are a safer habit.

Customers trust a label. What to put on your label
Product name and type (for example "Shea and Palm Bar Soap").

**Ingredients**, from largest to smallest. Handmade soap makers often list saponified oils by their international (INCI) names, such as Sodium Palmate (palm oil soap), Sodium Palm Kernelate, Sodium Shea Butterate and Sodium Castorate, plus Water, Glycerin and Fragrance.
**Net weight** after curing, for example 120 g. Weigh cured bars, not fresh ones.

Claims you must not make

Soap is a cosmetic: it cleans and can make skin feel soft. Saying a soap **treats or cures** a disease, such as "cures eczema", "kills infection" or "clears acne", is a medicinal claim. Drugs are regulated separately and more strictly. Stick to what you can honestly say: the oils you used, that it is handmade, the scent, and how it feels. Avoid "100% chemical free" too: everything, including water and soap, is a chemical, and every true soap was made with lye.
Allergens and fragrance

Some people react to fragrance and essential oils. List fragrance on the label and offer an unscented bar. Use fragrance only up to the supplier's stated maximum for soap, and never add bleaching agents or medicines to soap.

It protects you, because you can show NAFDAC inspectors, buyers or a supermarket that you work carefully. And it makes you better, because you can see exactly what changed between a good batch and a bad one.

Records for supplies, not only batches

Keep a simple purchase log too: date, item, supplier, quantity, price paid and any batch or lot number on the container. When a batch goes wrong, you can see whether it shared a new keg of palm oil or a new bag of caustic soda with other problem batches. The purchase log also feeds your costing in Module 4, because it shows exactly what each gram of oil costs you today, not what it cost three months ago.

Store your caustic soda receipts and supplier details with these records. It also helps when you train a helper: she can follow your written record instead of guessing.
Four numbers worth tracking
**Yield:** good bars per batch. Tells you whether cutting and moulds are consistent.
**Reject rate:** rejected bars divided by bars cut, times 100. Aim to bring it down batch by batch.
**Cure weight loss:** (weight at cutting minus cured weight) divided by weight at cutting, times 100. Tells you how much heavier to cut bars so the cured weight matches your label.
**Cost per good bar:** total batch cost divided by good bars. You will use this for pricing in Module 4.

Good soap only becomes a business when every bar is costed correctly, priced with a real profit, presented well and sold to people who come back. Many small makers price by guessing or by copying the seller next door. Then they discover, months later, that they were working for free. The fix is simple arithmetic you can do on your phone calculator. All naira figures in this lesson are **approximate examples**. Prices change quickly, so always use your own current market prices.
A bag of money
Profit is only what remains after ingredients, packaging, overheads and your labour are paid.
The four layers of cost
**Ingredients:** every oil, caustic soda, fragrance, colour, weighed per batch.
**Packaging:** wrapping paper or box, label, sticker, nylon or bag.
**Overheads:** a fair share of gas or fuel, water, gloves, pH strips, transport to the market, data for marketing.
**Labour:** your own time. If you do not pay yourself, the business is not really making money.
Ingredient cost from purchase price

To cost an ingredient, divide what you paid by the quantity you bought, then multiply by what you used. For example, if a 25 litre keg of palm oil costs a certain amount, find the cost per gram by weighing a known volume once, or ask the seller for the weight. Write down the cost per gram of each ingredient on a price sheet and update it whenever you restock.

Labour: 3 hours of making, cutting and wrapping at 1,000 naira per hour = 3,000 naira, or 300 naira per bar.
Full cost per bar: 900 + 300 = 1,200 naira.

Setting the price

If yours sits in that range and your quality and label are strong, keep it. If the market will not pay your price, reduce cost (cheaper fragrance, simpler wrap, bigger batches) rather than cutting your profit to nothing.

Packaging that works
**Only wrap cured bars.** Wrapping fresh soap traps moisture and can cause sweating and spots.
**Paper wraps or kraft boxes** let the soap breathe and look natural. Shrink wrap keeps scent in but can trap moisture in humid weather; test it first.
**One clear label** on every bar: name, ingredients, net weight, batch number, dates, contact.

Pick two brand colours and one font and use them on labels, price lists and Status posts. Do not rely on one channel. Many soap makers also sell at church or mosque events, women's association meetings, salons, and small supermarkets. Offer a small sample or a cut tester bar at stalls so people can smell and feel the soap.

What goes in your capstone pack

Writing your safety report

Keep it to one page. Describe your workspace and how you keep children and others away. List your protective equipment. Explain how you mix lye and in what order. Write your first aid steps. Record any near-miss honestly, for example a splash on the table or a moment you forgot goggles, and what you changed. A safety report that admits a near-miss and fixes it is stronger than one that claims nothing ever happens.
Getting useful feedback

Give two or three cured bars to people who will be honest with you, such as a neighbour, a hairdresser or a friend with sensitive skin. Ask them to use the soap for a week, then ask specific questions: How long did the bar last? Did it lather well in your water? Did your skin feel tight, itchy or fine? Did you like the smell? The simple picture
Soap is oil plus lye
Oils or fats + a strong alkali called lye
Bars: sodium hydroxide, or caustic soda
Liquid soap: potassium hydroxide, or KOH
The reaction is called saponification
Result: soap and glycerin, no lye left
Every true soap is made from two things. Fats or oils, and a strong alkali called lye.
For bar soap, the lye is sodium hydroxide. In our markets it is sold as caustic soda.
For soft and liquid soap, the lye is potassium hydroxide, often called caustic potash or K O H.
When oil and lye meet in water, they react. This is called saponification.
Oil and lye become soap and glycerin, a natural moisturiser. Measured correctly, no lye is left in the bar.
Choosing a method
Melt-and-pour or cold process?
With melt-and-pour, you melt a ready soap base. You never touch lye, but the base is costly.
Cold process needs care and about 4 to 6 weeks of curing, but gives the lowest cost per bar and full control. Most small soap businesses choose it.
Local oils
What each oil does in your bar
Palm oil: hard, long-lasting bar, 25% to 50%
Palm kernel oil: cleaning and lather, 15% to 30%
Shea butter: creamy and conditioning, 5% to 15%
Castor oil: boosts lather, 3% to 8%
Palm oil gives a hard, long-lasting bar with creamy lather. It can be 25% to 50% of your recipe.
Palm kernel oil, P K O, adds hardness, strong cleaning and big bubbles. Keep it at 15% to 30%, because too much can be drying.
Shea butter adds a creamy, conditioning feel, at 5% to 15%.
Castor oil boosts the lather, at 3% to 8%. Too much makes soap sticky.
Buy oils that smell fresh. Old oil causes orange spots later.

Why the maths matters
Getting the lye right keeps soap safe
Too much caustic soda: a harsh, burning bar
Too little: a greasy, soft bar that goes rancid
Calculate by hand, then check in SoapCalc
Never swap caustic soda and caustic potash
Getting the lye amount right is what makes soap safe. Too much caustic soda leaves a harsh bar that can burn.
Too little leaves a greasy, soft bar that may go rancid.
So you calculate by hand, to understand it, and then check in the free SoapCalc calculator, so you never rely on your arithmetic alone.
And caustic soda and caustic potash have different SAP values. A recipe made for one can never be used with the other.
Worked example
Amaka calculates her caustic soda
Each oil x its SAP value, e.g. palm 500 x 0.142
Add them up: 149.4 g at 0% superfat
Weigh 142 g caustic soda and 288 g water
Two calculations that agree give you confidence to mix.
For example, Amaka plans 1,000 g of oils. Palm oil 500 g, palm kernel oil 300 g, shea butter 150 g and castor oil 50 g.
Step one. Multiply each oil by its SAP value. Palm oil is 500 times 0.142, which is 71.0 g of caustic soda. She does the same for each oil.
Step two. Add them all up. 71.0, plus 52.8, plus 19.2, plus 6.4, gives 149.4 g.
Step three. Apply the superfat. Superfat is a little oil left on purpose as a safety margin. For 5%, multiply by 0.95. That gives 141.9 g.
Step four. Work out the water. Divide the lye by 0.33, which gives 430.0 g of solution, then take away the lye. That leaves 288.1 g of water.
So Amaka weighs 142 g of caustic soda and 288 g of water. Never round the lye up by more than a gram.
Then she enters the same recipe into SoapCalc. If the answers agree within a gram or two, she is ready. A big difference means a mistake.
Step by step
Making the batch
Safety gear on, mould lined, oils melted
Mix lye solution; cool both to 35 to 45 °C
Pour lye into oils; pulse 3 to 5 seconds, stir
Light trace: add fragrance, then pour
Rest 24 to 48 hours, cut, cure 4 to 6 weeks
Fresh soap is still caustic. Gloves on until it is curing.
Now the batch. Goggles, gloves and long sleeves on, children and pets out. Line your mould and gently melt the solid oils.
Add caustic soda to the water, in a ventilated place. Many beginners combine when the lye and oils are both between 35 and 45 degrees Celsius. Write both temperatures down.
Pour the lye slowly into the oils down the blender shaft. Pulse the stick blender for 3 to 5 seconds, stir, and repeat.
Stop at light trace, when a drizzle leaves a faint line on the surface, like thin custard. Add the fragrance and pour.
Leave it covered for 24 to 48 hours, away from children. Then cut into bars and cure them on a rack for 4 to 6 weeks, turning them every few days.
Until the reaction finishes, the batter can burn skin. Keep gloves on, and never let anyone touch or taste fresh soap.
If something looks wrong
Problems on the day
Sudden lumps (seizing): work fast, note fragrance
Oil pools and will not trace: check your weighing
Cracks or a wet dark patch: soap overheated
If the batter suddenly thickens and goes lumpy, called seizing, it is often the fragrance or mixing too hot. Press it into the mould quickly and note it in your record.
If oil pools on top and will not trace, check that you weighed the caustic soda correctly. If you are not sure, do not sell this batch.
Cracks or a dark wet patch after a day mean it overheated. In hot weather, skip the towel and keep the mould in a cool room.
Liquid soap
Cooked to a paste, then diluted
Needs a lye calculation
Keg liquid wash
People call two different products liquid soap. True liquid soap is cooked from oils and potassium hydroxide into a paste, then diluted with hot water. All the caustic soda safety rules apply.
The keg wash is a liquid detergent made from SLES, often sold as texapon. You dilute it in water and thicken it with salt, a little at a time. Too much salt makes it thin again.
Both can be good products. Just label each one honestly.
Stay safe
Three safety rules for liquid products
SLES paste irritates eyes and skin. Caustic potash needs full lye safety.
Use a cosmetic preservative at the supplier's stated rate. Never formalin.
Check a filled bottle daily for separation, cloudiness, smell or mould.
Wear gloves and goggles for both routes.
Some local recipes add formalin as a preservative. Formaldehyde is classified as a cancer-causing substance. Use a proper cosmetic preservative instead.
And test every new recipe for a week before you sell it, checking each day for separation, cloudiness, a smell change or mould.
Key points
Remember
Lye = oil weight x SAP value, for every oil
Check your hand calculation in SoapCalc
Combine at about 35 to 45 °C, cure 4 to 6 weeks
Liquid products need a proper preservative

Why this matters

Safe, consistent, honestly labelled
Fresh soap is not finished soap. Cold-process bars need 4 to 6 weeks of curing before you sell them.
During that time water slowly leaves the bar. It becomes harder, milder, and lasts longer in the soap dish.
Selling early may bring quick money, but it gives soft bars that melt away, and disappointed customers.
In this module you learn how to know a bar is truly ready: safe, consistent and honestly labelled.
Three tests
Weigh three marked bars every week. When the weight stops dropping, the water has gone.
A cured bar feels hard and does not dent easily with a fingernail.
Good handmade soap reads about pH 9 to 10. Clearly above 10: do not sell.
First, the weight test. Mark three bars from each batch and weigh them every week. When the weight stops dropping noticeably, most of the water has gone.
Second, the feel test. A cured bar is hard and does not dent easily with your fingernail. Wash your hands with it too. Skin should feel clean, not tight or stinging.
Third, the pH test. Wet the bar, rub a little lather, and press a pH strip into it. Well-made soap reads about 9 to 10.
A reading clearly above 10, especially with stinging, suggests too much lye. Do not sell that batch. Use strips, not your tongue.
Common faults
Safe to sell, or not?
Usually fine
White powder on top (soda ash)
Clear droplets in humid air
Cracks, if the pH is fine
Do not sell
White crunchy pockets inside
Oily layer or greasy patches
Stings, or pH clearly above 10
Some faults only affect looks. White powder on top is soda ash. Trim or wash it off once cured. Clear droplets come from humid air. Cracks mean overheating, so insulate less next time.
Others mean danger. White crunchy pockets inside can be undissolved caustic soda. Oily patches can mean too little lye or a weighing error.
When in doubt, do not sell it or give it away. Dispose of it wearing gloves. Your reputation depends on every bar being safe.
Honest labels
What your label must show
Product name and ingredients, largest first
Net weight after curing, e.g. 120 g
Your business name, address and phone
Batch number, date made, best-before date
Directions: for external use, avoid eyes
Customers trust a label. Start with the product name and the ingredients, from largest to smallest, including fragrance.
Give the net weight after curing, for example 120 g. Weigh cured bars, not fresh ones.
Add your business name, address and phone number.
Add the batch number, the date you made it, and a best-before date.
And a simple caution: for external use, avoid contact with eyes.
Never claim a soap treats or cures a disease, like eczema or acne. That is a medical claim. And avoid saying chemical free.
NAFDAC basics
The micro-scale NAFDAC path
Register your business name with CAC
Prepare a clean site and your documents
Apply on the NAFDAC online portal
Site inspection and sample analysis
Approval and your NAFDAC number
Confirm current fees with NAFDAC. Pay only official channels.
NAFDAC regulates soaps in Nigeria, and has a route for micro businesses with fewer than 10 employees. Step one is registering your business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission, CAC.
Step two. Separate soap making from cooking, in a clean room, and keep your batch records ready.
Step three. Apply online through the NAFDAC registration portal.
Step four. NAFDAC inspects your site, reviews your label and analyses your samples.
Step five. Approval, and your number goes on your label.
Fees change, so check the current amount on the NAFDAC website. Be careful of agents promising a number in days.
Worked example
Chinwe reads her batch records
CH-01: 10 bars cut, 2 rejected = 20%
CH-02 with a cutting guide: about 9%
Cure loss: 140 g to 128 g = about 8.6%
Label says 120 g, so she can cut smaller
Every batch gets a number and a written record: oils, weights, temperatures, bars cut and cure weights.
For example, Chinwe in Onitsha compares two batches of the same recipe.
Batch C H 01. 10 bars cut, 2 rejected for rough edges. Her reject rate is 20%.
For batch C H 02 she used a cutting guide. 11 bars, 1 rejected. About 9%. The guide halved her rejects.
Her marked bars weighed 140 g at cutting and 128 g after 5 weeks. That is a cure weight loss of about 8.6%.
Her label says 120 g, so she could cut slightly smaller bars, about 133 g fresh, and still meet her label weight.
Key points
Remember
Cure 4 to 6 weeks; weigh bars weekly
pH about 9 to 10; clearly higher means investigate
Crunchy pockets or oily patches: do not sell
Honest label, no medical claims
Number every batch and keep its record
To remember. Cure fully and weigh to confirm. Test the pH. Never sell a doubtful batch. Label honestly, without medical claims. And number every batch, so you can trace any problem in seconds.

Why this matters
Stop working for free
Guessing prices hides losses
Four layers: ingredients, packaging, overheads, labour
Your phone calculator is enough
Use your own current market prices
Many small makers price by guessing, or by copying the seller next door. Months later they discover they were working for free.
Every bar has four layers of cost. Ingredients, packaging, overheads like gas, water and transport, and your own labour. If you do not pay yourself, the business is not really making money.
The fix is simple arithmetic on your phone calculator.
All the naira figures here are approximate examples. Prices change quickly, so always use your own current prices.
Worked example
Amaka costs a 10-bar batch
For example, Amaka in Lagos costs her 1,000 g oil batch of 10 bars.
Packaging: wraps and labels
Overheads share
Naira prices are approximate.
For example, Amaka in Lagos makes 10 bars from a 1,000 g oil batch. Let us cost it.
Her oils, caustic soda and fragrance come to about 6,000 naira.
Printed wraps and labels for 10 bars are about 2,000 naira.
Her share of gas, water, gloves and transport is about 1,000 naira.
So the batch costs about 9,000 naira before labour. That is 900 naira per bar.
She also spends 3 hours at 1,000 naira per hour, which adds 300 naira per bar. Her full cost is about 1,200 naira per bar. Any price below that loses money.
Step by step
From full cost to a fair price
Price = full cost / (1 minus your margin)
Wholesale 20% off retail: 1,600 naira
Check similar handmade bars near you
Break-even: 30,000 / 800 = about 38 bars
Never price below your full cost per bar.
Now set the price. A simple formula: price equals full cost divided by 1 minus the margin you want.
For a 40% margin on 1,200 naira, divide by 0.60. That gives 2,000 naira, and 800 naira profit per bar.
A shop buying wholesale at 20% off pays 1,600 naira. You still make 400.
Then check what similar handmade bars sell for near you. If the market will not pay, cut costs, not your profit.
Finally, your start-up equipment. With 30,000 naira of equipment and 800 naira profit per bar, you must sell about 38 bars to get it back.
And use your real reject rate. If some bars are rejected, the cost of each good bar goes up.
Selling
Packaging, photos and WhatsApp
Wrap only cured bars, in paper or kraft boxes
Daylight photos on a plain background
WhatsApp Business catalogue and Status posts
Testers at church, mosque, salons and groups
Wrap only cured bars. Wrapping fresh soap traps moisture and causes sweating and spots. Paper wraps or kraft boxes let the soap breathe.
Take photos near a window in daylight, with no flash, on a plain background. Shoot the wrapped bar, the cut bar, and lather in hands. No filters that change the colour.
Use the free WhatsApp Business app for a catalogue with photos and prices. Post on your Status often.
Do not rely on one channel. Take tester bars to church or mosque events, women's meetings and salons, so people can smell and feel the soap.
Payment safety
Do
Check your own bank or Opay app
Agree delivery fees before payment
Keep customer numbers private
Never
Trust an SMS alert or screenshot
Share your PIN or one-time code
Add people to groups unasked
Before you release any soap, see the money in your own banking, Opay or Moniepoint app. Agree delivery fees first, and keep customer details private.
Fake bank alerts and edited screenshots are common. Never send goods because of an SMS or a picture. And never share your PIN or one-time code with anyone, even someone claiming to be your bank.
Your 90-day plan
Ngozi plans 60 bars in 90 days
Days 31 to 60: first sales, 25 bars
Days 61 to 90: 35 more bars, 10 wholesale
Production runs ahead of sales by the curing time.
Bars cure for 4 to 6 weeks, so soap you sell in month two must be made in month one.
For example, Ngozi in Enugu wants to sell 60 bars in her first 90 days.
In days 1 to 14 she makes two more batches of 10 bars, each with a batch record.
In days 15 to 30 she registers her business name, prints labels and confirms her cost at 1,200 naira a bar.
In days 31 to 60 her first batches are cured. She sells 25 bars through WhatsApp and her church group.
In days 61 to 90 she sells 35 more, including 10 at wholesale to a salon.
That is 116,000 naira in revenue, 72,000 in cost, and about 44,000 naira profit after paying herself.
Key points
Remember
Cost four layers, including your own labour
Full cost per bar = batch cost / good bars
Price = full cost / (1 minus margin)
Confirm payment in your own app first
Plan production ahead by the curing time

To remember. Cost all four layers, including your time. Divide by good bars, not perfect batches. Build your price from the cost up. Confirm every payment yourself. And plan production weeks ahead of sales.
